extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, War Department officials, and Army officers responsible for appointments, promotions, details, and status issues
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and legal standards governing vesting of military office, promotion, detail to staff, incompatibility with civil office, and related appointment procedures in the U.S. Army (historical opinions and statutory constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension from promotion for failing qualifying examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspension from promotion, upon failure to pass a qualifying examination, is in the nature of a penalty, and the suspension becomes operative when the right of the officer to promotion would have accrued had he passed a satisfactory examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such suspension runs for one year in any event, and until a vacancy occurs to which the officer can be appointed should he succeed in passing his examination. (C.15028, July 30, 1903; other cited opinions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No vested right in promotion as such
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no vested right in promotion as such on the part of officers of the Army; officers have promotion rights only under the law existing from time to time, and those rights vary with changes in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may alter commission dates or authorize new commissions that change precedence among officers; such legislative acts are within Congress's power even if they affect individual rights. (Example: Congress authorized issuance of a new commission giving precedence over others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment to vacancy among offices of same grade
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are two or more offices of the same grade in a corps, each requiring a separate commission, on a vacancy the appointing power may appoint the senior of the next lower grade to either office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 17 Op. Atty. Gen., 465 — illustrative of appointing discretion among equivalent vacancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office vests when appointing power fully exercised
rubrics_metrics.description: An office vests in the appointee when the appointing power has been fully exercised in respect thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vesting may occur on the date of appointment or commission, but is conditional on subsequent acceptance by the appointee. If the appointee dies before acceptance or before confirmation and acceptance (as in some cases), the office does not vest. (C.15262; C.28369; C.16359.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting conditional on acceptance; signing vs delivery of commission
rubrics_metrics.description: An appointment is complete when made out and signed by the appointing power and confers the right to the office, but the office is not considered filled until the appointee has, in fact, accepted it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Marbury v. Madison and other precedents show signing/sealing confers right but acceptance is required to consider the office filled; acceptance (or lack thereof) can defeat vesting if the appointee dies before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance may be treated as dating from assumption of duties
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer appointed to fill a vacancy entered upon the duties of his office on the vacancy date but did not communicate acceptance until later, the acceptance should be considered to date from the time he actually entered upon the duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.27305, Sept. 27, 1910 — practical rule treating de facto assumption of duties as effective acceptance for dating purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion by operation of law (duration of service)
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain categories (e.g., assistant surgeons and lieutenants of engineers and ordnance), promotion to a higher grade may result by operation of law from mere duration of service and independently of action by the appointing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.43, 208, Feb. 1880 — recognizes statutory, automatic advancement separate from presidential appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion subject to appointment/confirmation/commission (transfers after exam)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing an examination alone does not make an officer an officer of a new corps by mere transfer; he must be appointed, confirmed, and commissioned in the usual way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: passing Ordnance Corps exam does not suffice to become an ordnance officer without appointment/confirmation/commission. (P.37.156, Dec. 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of transfers/exchanges on rights under reorganization acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where officers effect mutual transfers before a reorganization act takes effect, a transferee may succeed to rights that vested in the other officer when the reorganization became operative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Lieut. D. who exchanged with Lieut. M. succeeded to all advancement rights vested in Lieut. M. when the Artillery reorganization became operative. (C.21053, Apr. 9, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail to staff vests staff office and creates vacancy in line
rubrics_metrics.description: A line officer detailed for duty in a staff department becomes during such detail an officer of that staff department; the vacancy created in the line has been filled by promotion, and the officer's commission in the line remains dormant while he holds the staff office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The staff office vests on the date of detail order; the detailed officer's status in the staff is as fully vested as if appointment were permanent. (Section 16, act of Feb. 2, 1901; C. U018, Jan. 22, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Command authority and limitations while detailed to staff
rubrics_metrics.description: While detailed to a staff department, the officer occupies the same status in respect to exercise of command as other officers of that staff—he can exercise command in his own department but is inhibited from exercising command elsewhere in the military establishment except by presidential assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A detailed officer is not entitled, as a line officer, to assume and exercise the command provided for in the 122nd article of war. (C. U018, Jan. 22, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting date and statutory tour for General Staff details
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer detailed as a member of the General Staff vests in the office on the date of the order promulgating the detail, and the statutory tour of duty for General Staff is four years after that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.15844, Jan. 21, 1904; C.22482, Dec. 2, 1907 — establishes vesting and a fixed four-year term unless sooner relieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-year limit on General Staff details and redetail rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Section (act of Feb. 14, 1903) requires that officers detailed in the General Staff Corps be detailed for periods of four years unless sooner relieved; it forbids employment for periods differing from or in excess of those provided by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At end of statutory tour, further continuance is without authority and the Secretary of War must issue orders for relief; an officer relieved before completing four years may be redetailed to finish an unexpired term but becomes ineligible after completing a total of four years. (C.24868, Apr. 30, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of detailed staff officers for General Staff detail
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the line serving in the detailed staff is eligible, while so serving, for detail in the General Staff; officers serving in the detailed staff, equally with officers of the line and staff, constitute the Army at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language authorizing details 'from the Army at large' supports eligibility. (C.20140, July 26, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion while detailed requires separation from staff if numbers would exceed authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: When the right of a detailed officer to promotion in the line has accrued, such promotion involves his separation from the staff department in which he is serving if his retention would increase the number of staff officers in the higher grade beyond the number expressly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes prescribing the number of officers in each grade of a department prevent retention on staff when promotion would create an excess. (C.10004; other cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Directory character of certain detail requirements and emergency relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of sections 26 and 27 (act of Feb. 2, 1901) establishing the detail system are directory in character; when, in the Secretary of War's opinion, an emergency requires resort to detail, an officer detailed on that basis may be relieved and replaced by an officer of like arm and qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary's discretion in emergencies allows deviations from strict prescription when necessary. (C.11466, Feb. 11, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail does not prevent transfers within the line
rubrics_metrics.description: Being detailed in a staff department does not operate to prevent an officer from effecting a transfer as a line officer with an officer of equal grade in the line of the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.21783 and related opinions confirm transfer rights notwithstanding detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain positions (veterinarians, paymasters' clerks) are appointed by Secretary of War and are inferior officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Veterinarians authorized for cavalry and artillery regiments are actual incumbents of military office inducted by the Secretary of War and are not commissioned officers appointed by the President; paymasters' clerks in the Army are inferior officers appointed by the Secretary of War under the Constitution's appointment clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.8587, Oct. 10, 1910; C.10603, July 7 & Oct. 7, 1911. Distinguishes types of appointment and entitlement to leaves/pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration to service requires a new appointment; dismissal revocation is ineffectual
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer dismissed or otherwise separated from the Army (summary dismissal, wholly retired, resignation accepted) is a civilian and can be readmitted only by a new appointment under the Constitution; revocation of the original separation order is null and without effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1228 R.S. and multiple historical opinions state President cannot restore without compliance with constitutional appointment process; prior opinions cited: R.35, 466; R.37, 451; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding incompatible offices vacates prior office
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person holding one office enters upon another office the performance of whose duties is incompatible with the first, he abandons and vacates the first office upon entering the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two offices are incompatible if performance of one will prevent or conflict with performance of the other or is contrary to law's policy; acceptance of the incompatible position is treated as resignation/abandonment. (Crosthwaite v. U.S.; Digest of 2d Comp. Dec.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1222 R.S.: prohibition on holding civil office while on active list
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1222 R.S. provides that no officer of the Army on the active list shall hold any civil office, and every such officer who accepts or exercises the functions of a civil office shall thereby cease to be an officer of the Army and his commission shall be vacated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is an exercise of Congress's power to raise armies. 'Exercising the functions of a civil office' means transacting the business by virtue of holding the office (more than mere agency). Examples: honorary militia titles without functions may not vacate; holding civil office created by State or municipality will vacate. (C.272; opinions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'civil office' under section 1222
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'civil office' embraces Federal, State, Territorial, and municipal office and also certain cases of public civil employment; to bring an office within section 1222 it is necessary that the civil office be created by Congress, a State or municipality (i.e., a public civil office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases list park commissioner, county physician, trustee of a railroad, membership on sanitary commission, assistant to postmaster, etc., as civil offices that would vacate military commission. (R.36; C.19350; C.18017; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing temporary employment/contractual service from civil office
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary employment or purely contractual services (e.g., being employed by a board to devise sewerage, consulting engineer engagement, rendering medical services to prisoners) are not necessarily 'civil offices' under section 1222 and do not necessarily vacate military commission when done with Secretary of War approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: employment by board of supervisors to devise sewerage considered temporary employment, not civil office (0.23931; P.54, 64). Consulting or temporary State employment distinguished from statutory public office. Medical services to prisoners treated as contractual (C.27213, Aug. 29, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of certain militia commissions or honorary positions may not vacate commission
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a commission in the Organized Militia, or honorary titles/commissions that carry no tenure, pay, emoluments, rights, powers or duties outside a limited context, does not constitute a civil office that vacates an Army commission under section 1222.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commissions in Organized Militia or honorary commission in a state military school (C.25242; C.29273; C.18017). Distinguish functional civil offices from honorary or incidental militia positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of assignments under Volunteer acts differs from appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under acts authorizing assignment of staff officers to volunteer forces, acceptance of such an assignment by a Regular officer does not vacate his Regular commission, and nomination/confirmation is not required for Regular officers 'assigned' in this manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 10, act of Apr. 22, 1898 — accepting assignment as provided does not vacate Regular commission; assignments are discretionary and not the same as presidential appointment requiring Senate confirmation. (G.4449, May 19, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-duty private activities permitted if they do not impair military duties
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer may invest private funds and may serve as a director in a business corporation provided the performance of his military duties is not impaired or prevented by such service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.22765, Feb. 17, 1908 — private investments and corporate directorship acceptable so long as military duties remain unimpaired; separate from holding a public civil office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission language 'subject to examination' cannot be altered after vesting
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer was advanced without examination and the words 'subject to examination' were placed on his commission, once the office had vested no different commission could be issued omitting those words without another exercise of the constitutional appointing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After vesting, a new commission that materially changes the original would require re-exercise of appointment power. (C.19267, Feb. 27, 1906.)
